canonical_topic: Energy density comparison: gasoline vs. natural gas
definition: A worked comparison of storage volume needed for equivalent heat energy from gasoline versus natural gas in various forms (atmospheric, compressed, liquefied).
core_idea: Gasoline is far more energy-dense by volume than natural gas at atmospheric pressure, and even substantial compression or liquefaction does not fully close that gap.
key_points: One gallon of gasoline contains about 124,000 Btu and occupies about 0.13 cubic feet
The same amount of energy in natural gas at standard atmospheric pressure requires about 100 cubic feet of storage

At about 250 times atmospheric pressure (roughly comparable to scuba tank compression levels of 200-300x), natural gas still needs about three times the storage volume of gasoline, plus a heavy pressurized cylinder
As supercooled liquid (LNG), natural gas holds about two-thirds the energy per volume of gasoline
relationships: Illustrates numerically why natural gas transport/storage logistics (pipeline, compression, or liquefaction) differ fundamentally from liquid fuels like gasoline
trading_implications: Explains why natural gas vehicles/storage face practical volume/weight penalties compared to liquid fuels, relevant to any gas-as-transport-fuel economics
caveats: Assuming compression alone (e.g., to scuba-tank-like pressures) brings natural gas storage density close to gasoline; the source shows it still needs roughly 3x the volume even at ~250x atmospheric pressure
